To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

students' emotions have important effects on achievement and self regulated learning, and that these effects can be predicted by students' perceptions of the control-value structure of academic situations.

(a) academic emotions are related to students' self regulated learning and achievement; (b) the relations are mediated by motivational and control processes, and moderated by personality and contextual factors; and (c) academic emotions are a function of students' achievement and motivational goals, their beliefs about their own ability and effort, and their perceptions of classroom structure and social environment.

(1) students experience a wide range of positive and negative emotions in academic settings, (2) these emotions are related to students' motivational and cognitive resources, self-regulated learning, and academic achievement; (3) they have both adaptive and maladaptive functions, and (4) their experience is affected by students' personal dispositions, as well as classroom factors.
